summary: The non_gaia project implements the cockroach-detection system using the crewai framework, with four agents (SensorAgent, CoordinatorAgent, AlertingAgent, NotificationAgent) structured as plain Python classes. All seven functional requirements are at least partially covered through direct method calls, but the crewai integration is entirely non-functional: the Crew is instantiated with plain Python objects instead of crewai Agent instances, tasks list is empty, and crew.kickoff() is never called. Additionally, the system is inconsistently named 'RatDetectionSystem' with internal references to 'rats' rather than cockroaches throughout, and SensorData is defined in two separate files.

findings.description: The crewai Crew is constructed with plain Python class instances (SensorAgent, CoordinatorAgent, AlertingAgent, NotificationAgent) that do not inherit from crewai.Agent. crewai will raise a validation error when the Crew is used, and crew.kickoff() is never called anyway, making the framework integration inert.
findings.evidence: main.py lines 24-28: `self.crew = Crew(agents=[self.sensor1, self.coordinator, self.alerting, self.notification], tasks=[])`; none of the agent classes inherit from crewai.Agent

findings.description: There is no agent-to-agent communication. All interaction is via direct Python method calls on object references held by RatDetectionSystem. The crewai messaging or task-passing infrastructure is completely bypassed.
findings.evidence: main.py lines 46-63: coordinator, alerting, and notification methods are called directly — no message passing, no crewai task delegation

findings.description: Sensor data transmission is not periodic. Sensors are polled synchronously inside a for-loop with time.sleep(1), not driven by independent periodic agents, violating the requirement that each sensor device regularly transmits data autonomously.
findings.evidence: main.py lines 72-81: `for i in range(5): data_list = self.generate_sensor_data(); self.process_data(data_list); time.sleep(1)`

findings.description: Pattern analysis is statistical only and contains no temporal pattern recognition. The system computes averages and maximums per location but does not identify emergence patterns over time.
findings.evidence: coordinator_agent.py lines 26-44: analyze_patterns() computes total_events, avg_rats, max_rats — no time-series or trend analysis

findings.description: Student room notifications are only sent when rat_count > 0 (meaning any detection triggers an alert path), but the room status update uses 'warning' only for count >= 5 and 'safe' otherwise — students in rooms with 1-4 cockroaches receive a 'safe' status message, which contradicts the requirement to inform students of a bad condition.

SensorData is defined twice: once in utils/data_models.py and again in agents/sensor_agent.py with identical fields. main.py imports from utils.data_models but sensor_agent.py uses its own local definition, creating two distinct types with the same name.
findings.evidence: utils/data_models.py lines 6-10 and agents/sensor_agent.py lines 6-10 both define `class SensorData(BaseModel)` with identical fields

findings.description: The system class and all internal terminology refer to 'rats' rather than cockroaches, inconsistent with the stated requirements for a cockroach-infestation monitoring system.
findings.evidence: main.py line 12: `class RatDetectionSystem`; coordinator_agent.py line 22: `{data.rat_count} rats`; sensor_agent.py line 21: `rat_count = random.randint(...)`

findings.description: The analyze_sensor_data and identify_hotspots functions in utils/analysis.py duplicate logic already present in CoordinatorAgent.analyze_patterns() and CoordinatorAgent.identify_hotspots(), and the utility functions are never called anywhere.
findings.evidence: utils/analysis.py lines 6-44 vs coordinator_agent.py lines 26-55 — identical statistical logic; neither main.py nor any agent imports utils.analysis

findings.description: `from pydantic import BaseModel` is imported in alerting_agent.py and notification_agent.py but neither file defines or uses a Pydantic model.
findings.evidence: agents/alerting_agent.py line 1: `from pydantic import BaseModel`; agents/notification_agent.py line 1: `from pydantic import BaseModel`

findings.description: Public methods across all agent files lack type annotations on return types.
findings.evidence: coordinator_agent.py line 12: `def receive_data(self, data):` — no return type; alerting_agent.py line 12: `def send_alert(self, alert_data):` — no return type

findings.description: The Crew dependency (crewai, openai) is listed in requirements.txt but the framework is not meaningfully used, adding heavy dependencies for no functional benefit.
findings.evidence: requirements.txt: `crewai>=0.14.0`, `openai>=1.30.5`; crew is never kicked off in main.py

logical_inconsistencies: Crew is instantiated with non-crewai objects and an empty task list; crew.kickoff() is never called, making the declared multi-agent framework entirely unused.
SensorData is defined in two modules; the type used by CoordinatorAgent is the local one from sensor_agent.py, not the one from utils/data_models.py that main.py imports.
Rooms with 1-4 detected cockroaches receive a 'safe' status notification, directly contradicting the requirement to inform students of bad conditions.
analyze_sensor_data() and identify_hotspots() utilities are defined but never imported or called, rendering them dead code.
implementation_risks: Passing plain Python instances to crewai.Crew will raise a Pydantic validation error if crew.kickoff() is ever called, breaking the intended orchestration path.
Synchronous polling with time.sleep(1) blocks the main thread; adding more sensors or longer processing will cause noticeable lag and is not scalable.
No tests exist; the duplicate SensorData definitions could cause silent type mismatches if the two classes diverge.
openai dependency is pulled in but no LLM key configuration is provided; crewai will fail to initialise agents if kickoff is attempted without a valid API key.
